questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Member eligibility
questions.question: A listed company's board wants a director on its audit committee who also earns a consulting fee from a company subsidiary. Under Rule 10A-3, which statement is MOST accurate?

options.A: The director may serve once shareholders are told about the fee
options.B: The director may serve only after the fee arrangement ends
options.C: The director may serve because they are not a company employee
options.D: The director may serve because a subsidiary, not the issuer, pays

questions.key_concept: An audit committee member may take no consulting, advisory or other compensatory fee from the issuer or any subsidiary.
questions.pre_read: Recall which payments Rule 10A-3 lets a committee member receive, and from which companies in the group.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10A-3 bars an audit committee member from accepting any consulting, advisory or other compensatory fee, directly or indirectly, from the issuer or any subsidiary, other than for board and committee service. The consulting fee therefore disqualifies the director while it continues. Option D fails because the rule names subsidiaries expressly, so which company in the group pays makes no difference.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure fixes many governance gaps. But independence is a listing condition; telling shareholders about the fee does not make the director independent.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because employees plainly lack independence. But Rule 10A-3 also bars consulting and advisory fees and affiliate status, so non-employees can fail too.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the fee does come from a subsidiary. But Rule 10A-3 covers fees from the issuer or any subsidiary, so the payer changes nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Disclosure does not cure a failed independence test, and Rule 10A-3 looks beyond employment to any consulting or advisory fee.
Final two: B beats D because the fee ban covers payments from the issuer or any of its subsidiaries.
Exam cue: for audit committee independence, any non-board fee from the company group disqualifies the member, whatever the amount or which entity pays.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Accounting dispute
questions.question: At a listed company, the CFO and the independent auditor disagree on when to recognize revenue from a large contract. Under Section 301, who is directly responsible for resolving the disagreement?

options.A: The CFO, who prepares the financial statements
options.B: The PCAOB, which inspects and disciplines the audit firm
options.C: The full board of directors, which appoints the committees
options.D: The audit committee, which oversees the audit firm's work

questions.key_concept: The audit committee oversees the auditor's work, including resolving financial reporting disagreements between management and the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Identify which body Section 301 makes directly responsible for the auditor's work, and what that oversight includes.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 301 makes the audit committee, acting as a committee of the board, directly responsible for overseeing the audit firm's work, including resolving disagreements between management and the auditor about financial reporting. The firm reports directly to the committee. A listed company must have an audit committee, and the Act places this duty on that committee rather than on the board as a whole.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the CFO prepares the numbers in dispute. But the CFO is one side of the disagreement; Section 301 gives its resolution to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees audit firms. But it inspects and disciplines firms; it does not settle a company's accounting disputes with its auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the audit committee is a committee of the board. But Section 301 assigns oversight of the auditor, including disputes, directly to the audit committee.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. The CFO is one side of the dispute, and the PCAOB regulates audit firms rather than resolving a client's reporting disagreements.
Final two: D beats C because Section 301 places oversight of the auditor, including management-auditor disputes, on the audit committee itself.
Exam cue: hiring, paying, overseeing or refereeing the independent auditor points to the audit committee, not management; the whole board steps in only when an issuer has no audit committee.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Employee concerns
questions.question: An employee at a listed company wants to report questionable accounting without giving their name. What does Section 301 require?

options.A: Audit committee procedures for anonymous submission
options.B: An anonymous hotline run by the independent auditor
options.C: An internal audit unit taking anonymous reports
options.D: An anonymous reporting line straight to the SEC

questions.key_concept: Audit committees must set procedures for accounting complaints and for employees' confidential, anonymous submission of concerns.
questions.pre_read: Recall which body owns the complaint procedures and what employees must be able to do through them.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 301 requires each audit committee to set procedures for the confidential, anonymous submission by employees of concerns about questionable accounting or auditing, alongside procedures for complaints the company receives. The committee owns the procedures; staff or a vendor may run them. SOX itself does not require an internal audit function, so an internal audit team is not what the section demands.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the audit firm is independent of management. But Section 301 puts the anonymous channel under the audit committee's procedures, not the independent auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: internal audit often takes reports. But Section 301 requires procedures set by the audit committee; SOX does not itself require an internal audit function.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC accepts anonymous tips. But that is a separate whistleblower route; Section 301 requires an internal channel set by the audit committee.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Section 301 places the channel under the audit committee, so neither the audit firm's hotline nor a line to the SEC is what it requires.
Final two: A beats C because Section 301 makes the audit committee set the procedures, and SOX does not mandate an internal audit function.
Exam cue: anonymous employee concerns about accounting point to the audit committee's Section 301 complaint procedures.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Disclosures behind the signature
questions.question: Before signing the quarterly Section 302 certification, a CFO learns that the assistant controller, who approves journal entries, took $8,000 from petty cash, an immaterial amount. What is the MOST accurate requirement?

options.A: Leave it out of the disclosures, since the amount is immaterial
options.B: Report it in the Section 906 statement furnished with the report
options.C: Disclose it to the auditors and the audit committee
options.D: Disclose it as a material weakness in the 10-Q

questions.key_concept: Officers disclose to the auditors and audit committee any fraud, material or not, involving management or key internal control staff.
questions.pre_read: Note the employee's role in internal control, then recall what the certification says officers have disclosed, and to whom.
questions.correct_explanation: The Section 302 certification states that the signing officers have disclosed to the auditors and the audit committee any fraud, whether or not material, involving management or other employees with a significant role in internal control. An assistant controller who approves journal entries has that role. The rule calls for disclosure to those two parties; it does not turn an immaterial theft into a publicly reported material weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because most disclosure turns on materiality. But the 302 certification covers fraud by key control staff whether or not it is material.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because 906 is also an officer certification. But the 906 statement covers compliance and fair presentation, not reporting fraud to anyone.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the theft may signal a control deficiency. But the certification requires disclosure to the auditors and audit committee; it does not label this a material weakness.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. The 302 duty covers fraud by key control staff even when immaterial, and the 906 statement contains no fraud disclosure.
Final two: C beats D because the certification sends insider fraud to the auditors and audit committee without making an immaterial theft a public material weakness.
Exam cue: fraud by management or key control staff, material or not, goes to the auditors and audit committee under Section 302.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Penalty tier
questions.question: A CEO willfully certifies a Section 906 statement knowing the periodic report does not comply with the Exchange Act. What is the GREATEST criminal penalty the statute allows?

options.A: Up to $1 million in fines and 10 years in prison
options.B: Up to $5 million in fines and 20 years in prison
options.C: Repayment of bonuses received in the following 12 months
options.D: A civil money penalty and a bar from serving as an officer

questions.key_concept: Section 906 has two criminal tiers: knowing certification up to $1 million and 10 years; willful up to $5 million and 20 years.
questions.pre_read: Find the word in the stem that tells you which of the statute's two penalty tiers applies.
questions.correct_explanation: 18 U.S.C. 1350, added by Section 906, has two penalty tiers. Knowingly certifying a noncompliant report carries fines up to $1 million, prison up to 10 years, or both. Willfully certifying it, as here, carries fines up to $5 million, prison up to 20 years, or both. The word willfully in the stem selects the higher tier.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is the 906 penalty for knowing certification. Willful certification moves to the higher tier of $5 million and 20 years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because repayment follows misconduct restatements. But that is Section 304, a civil reimbursement duty, not the criminal penalty for a false 906 certification.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the SEC can seek bars and civil penalties. But the question asks for the criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. 1350, which means fines and prison.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Bonus repayment is Section 304 and bars are civil remedies, while Section 906 sets criminal fines and prison.
Final two: B beats A because willful certification carries the higher tier; $1 million and 10 years applies to knowing certification.
Exam cue: for Section 906, knowing means up to $1 million and 10 years; willful means up to $5 million and 20 years.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Quarterly filing contents
questions.question: Preparing a Form 10-Q, a CFO plans to attach Section 302 and 906 certifications and include a Section 404 management report on internal control. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Drop the 404 report, which goes with the annual report alone
options.B: Drop the 906 statement, which goes with the annual report alone
options.C: Drop the 302 certification, which goes with the annual report alone
options.D: Keep the three items, since each is required in every quarterly report

questions.key_concept: Sections 302 and 906 certifications go with quarterly and annual reports; the Section 404(a) management report is annual only.
questions.pre_read: For each of the three items, recall which periodic reports the statute names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) requires management's internal control report in each annual report only, so it does not belong in a Form 10-Q. Section 302 covers each annual and quarterly report, and Section 906 (18 U.S.C. 1350) covers every periodic report containing financial statements, which includes a 10-Q. Both certifications stay; only the 404 report comes out.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: some link the criminal 906 statement to the 10-K alone. But 18 U.S.C. 1350 covers every periodic report with financial statements, including a 10-Q.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because annual reports carry the most certifications. But Section 302 expressly covers each annual or quarterly report.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because all three are SOX duties. But Section 404(a) asks for management's internal control report in the annual report, not each quarter.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 302 names quarterly reports expressly, and the Section 404 management report is an annual requirement.
Final two: A beats B because 18 U.S.C. 1350 reaches every periodic report with financial statements, while 404(a) is annual.
Exam cue: on a 10-Q, look for the 302 and 906 certifications; the 404 internal control report appears once a year, in the 10-K.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Conduct toward the auditor
questions.question: Following the CEO's direction, a regional sales vice president hides from the auditors a side letter giving a customer return rights, to keep revenue in the quarter. Which provision MOST directly prohibits this?

options.A: Section 304, which makes officers repay bonuses after misconduct
options.B: Section 302, which requires officers to disclose fraud to auditors
options.C: Section 307, which requires lawyers to report violations internally
options.D: Section 303, which bars misleading the auditor to distort statements

questions.key_concept: Section 303 bars officers, directors and those acting under their direction from fraudulently misleading or pressuring the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Ask which provision is aimed at conduct toward the auditor, and whether it reaches staff acting on an officer's instructions.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 303 makes it unlawful for an officer or director, or anyone acting under their direction, to fraudulently influence, coerce, manipulate or mislead the auditor to make the financial statements materially misleading. Hiding a side letter on the CEO's direction fits that prohibition. Section 302 is an officer certification that includes disclosing fraud; it does not itself prohibit misleading the auditor.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because misconduct can lead to repayment. But Section 304 applies after a misconduct restatement and recovers CEO and CFO pay; it does not prohibit misleading auditors.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: officers certify they disclosed fraud to the auditors. But that is a certification duty; Section 303 is the provision that prohibits misleading the auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it concerns reporting violations. But Section 307 sets duties for attorneys practicing before the SEC, not for sales staff dealing with auditors.

tips: Eliminate: A and C. Section 304 recovers pay after a restatement, and Section 307 governs attorneys' internal reporting, not conduct toward auditors.
Final two: D beats B because Section 303 prohibits misleading the auditor, and it reaches anyone acting under an officer's direction.
Exam cue: pressure on, or deception of, the independent auditor by insiders or their staff points to Section 303.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Amounts repaid
questions.question: A company restates its financial statements because misconduct caused material noncompliance with reporting requirements. Under Section 304, which CEO and CFO amounts must be reimbursed?

options.A: Base salary paid for each period the restatement covers
options.B: Incentive pay received in the three fiscal years before the restatement
options.C: Bonuses and stock-sale profits in the 12 months after first issuance
options.D: Any pay the audit committee links to the misconduct

questions.key_concept: Section 304 recovers CEO and CFO bonuses, incentive or equity pay and stock-sale profits from 12 months after first issuance.
questions.pre_read: Recall the look-back window Section 304 uses and the kinds of pay it reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 304 requires the CEO and CFO to reimburse bonuses and other incentive-based or equity-based pay received, and profits from selling company stock, during the 12 months after the misstated document was first publicly issued or filed. The three-year look-back reaching every executive officer belongs to the Rule 10D-1 recovery policy, a separate no-fault listing rule.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because salary is the largest pay item. But Section 304 reaches bonuses, incentive or equity pay and stock-sale profits, not base salary.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: that is Rule 10D-1, which needs no misconduct and reaches every executive officer. Section 304 covers the CEO and CFO for 12 months after first issuance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the audit committee oversees reporting. But Section 304 sets the amounts by statute; it does not leave them to committee judgment.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 304 does not reach base salary, and the statute, not the audit committee, defines what is repaid.
Final two: C beats B because Section 304 uses the 12 months after first issuance; the three-year look-back is the Rule 10D-1 policy.
Exam cue: misconduct restatement plus CEO and CFO plus a 12-month window points to Section 304, not the Rule 10D-1 clawback.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Trade during a plan freeze
questions.question: During a ten-business-day freeze that stops every 401(k) participant from trading company stock, a director sells shares received as director pay, at a profit. What is the MOST accurate consequence?

options.A: The director's profit from the sale belongs to the issuer
options.B: The SEC must sue within 60 days to recover the profit
options.C: The sale stands, since the director meant no harm
options.D: The sale stands, since the director has no plan account

questions.key_concept: Profits from a director's or executive officer's trade during a pension blackout belong to the issuer, regardless of intent.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the freeze is a blackout under the statute, then recall who is restricted and who gets any profit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 306(a) makes it unlawful for a director or executive officer to sell stock acquired through that service during a blackout of more than three business days affecting at least half of plan participants. Any profit belongs to the issuer, whatever the director intended. The issuer recovers it; a shareholder may sue on the issuer's behalf if the issuer does not act within 60 days of a request.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: 60 days does appear in Section 306. But it is the time the issuer has before a shareholder may sue; the profit goes to the issuer.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because many violations require intent. But Section 306(a) makes the profit recoverable irrespective of the director's intention.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the freeze affects plan participants. But the trading ban applies to directors and executive officers whether or not they hold plan accounts.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 306(a) disregards intent, and the ban reaches directors and executive officers whether or not they are plan participants.
Final two: A beats B because the profit belongs to the issuer, and 60 days is when a shareholder may sue on its behalf.
Exam cue: an insider trade during a pension blackout means the issuer recovers the profit, regardless of intent.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Attorneys and fair funds. First report
questions.question: An outside lawyer representing a listed company with no qualified legal compliance committee finds evidence of a material securities violation. Under Section 307, where must the lawyer report FIRST?

options.A: To the audit committee of the board of directors
options.B: To the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO
options.C: To the SEC's Division of Enforcement, in writing
options.D: Nowhere, because legal privilege keeps the evidence confidential

questions.key_concept: An attorney's report of a material violation goes first to the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, then up the ladder.
questions.pre_read: Recall the order of the reporting ladder the Section 307 rule sets, and when the second rung applies.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 307 required SEC rules making an attorney who practices before the SEC for an issuer report evidence of a material violation up the ladder. Under 17 CFR 205.3(b), the first report goes to the chief legal officer, or to that officer and the CEO. Only if they fail to respond appropriately does the report go to the audit committee, another independent committee or the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the audit committee is the second rung. The rule sends the report there only after no appropriate response, or when reporting first would be futile.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC enforces securities law. But Section 307 sets an internal reporting ladder; it does not require a first report to the SEC.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because lawyers protect client confidences. But the rule requires reporting inside the company, and doing so does not breach privilege.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The Section 307 rule keeps the report inside the company, and reporting to its officers does not breach client confidences.
Final two: B beats A because the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, comes first; the audit committee is the next rung.
Exam cue: attorney evidence of a violation climbs the ladder: the chief legal officer, alone or with the CEO, first; then the audit committee, another independent committee or the board.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Attorneys and fair funds. Where a penalty goes
questions.question: The SEC obtains a civil penalty against a former CFO who misled investors. Under Section 308, what may the SEC do with the penalty?

options.A: Pay it to the U.S. Treasury, apart from any victims' fund
options.B: Pay it to the company to make up its own losses
options.C: Pay it to the PCAOB to fund audit firm inspections
options.D: Add it to a disgorgement or other fund for the victims

questions.key_concept: Under Section 308, the SEC can add a civil penalty to a disgorgement fund or other fund for the violation's victims.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Section 308 was written to benefit and what it allows the SEC to do with penalty money.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 308(a), as amended by Dodd-Frank Section 929B, lets the SEC, on its motion or at its direction, add any civil penalty it obtains, by order or settlement, to a disgorgement fund or other fund for the victims of the violation. Since 2010 no disgorgement order is needed. Fair funds are an exception to penalties going to the U.S. Treasury.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: civil penalties generally go to the Treasury. But Section 308 lets the SEC add the penalty to a fund for the victims instead.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the company may have been harmed too. But Section 308 directs the money toward the investors who were victims of the violation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the PCAOB oversees auditors. But Section 308 concerns SEC actions against violators and funds for their victims, not PCAOB funding.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Fair funds serve the investors harmed by a violation, not the company's own losses or the PCAOB's budget.
Final two: D beats A because Section 308 lets the SEC add civil penalties to a disgorgement or other fund for victims, instead of the Treasury.
Exam cue: a civil penalty steered to harmed investors through a fund points to Section 308 fair funds; no disgorgement order is needed.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Credit to an executive
questions.question: A retail chain that issues its own credit cards to shoppers reviews four proposals for its CFO. Under Section 402, which arrangement is permitted?

options.A: A low-rate relocation loan made through a foreign subsidiary
options.B: A personal loan the company arranges with a partner bank
options.C: A card account on the terms offered to the general public
options.D: A pre-2002 personal loan renewed this year on better terms

questions.key_concept: Section 402 bars personal loans to directors and executive officers, except ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms.
questions.pre_read: Recall the ways of providing credit Section 402 prohibits, and the conditions of its consumer credit exception.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 402 bars an issuer, directly or through a subsidiary, from extending, arranging or renewing personal loans to directors and executive officers. It excepts consumer credit, such as a credit card, made in the ordinary course of the issuer's consumer credit business, generally offered to the public, on terms no better than the public receives. A card account on public terms fits that exception; arranging a bank loan does not.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a foreign subsidiary seems outside the rule. But Section 402 covers credit extended directly or indirectly, including through any subsidiary.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the bank, not the company, would lend. But Section 402 also prohibits arranging an extension of credit for a director or executive officer.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because older loans were grandfathered. But that protection ends if the loan is renewed or materially modified after the Act.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 402 reaches credit through any subsidiary, and renewing an older loan ends its grandfathered status.
Final two: C beats B because ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms is excepted, while arranging a loan is itself prohibited.
Exam cue: an insider loan is barred whether made, arranged or renewed; ordinary-course consumer credit on public terms is the exception.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Reporting deadline
questions.question: A director of a listed company buys company shares on a Monday. Under Section 403, by when must the director report the purchase?

options.A: Within 10 days after the end of the month of the trade
options.B: Before the end of the second business day after the trade
options.C: Within 10 days after the director first joined the board
options.D: With the company's next quarterly report on Form 10-Q

questions.key_concept: Insiders report a change in ownership before the end of the second business day after the trade.
questions.pre_read: Separate the deadline for a first statement on becoming an insider from the deadline for later trades.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 403 rewrote Exchange Act Section 16(a). A director, officer or owner of more than 10 percent must report a change in ownership before the end of the second business day after the trade is executed, unless the SEC sets another time where two days is not feasible. Ten days applies to the initial statement after becoming an insider, not to later trades.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this was Section 16(a)'s deadline before 2002. Section 403 replaced it with a report before the end of the second business day after the trade.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because 10 days is a real Section 16(a) deadline. But it applies to the initial statement after becoming a director, not to later trades.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because quarterly reports disclose many changes. But insider ownership changes are filed separately and quickly, not with the Form 10-Q.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Ten days covers the initial statement on becoming an insider, and insider trades are reported separately from the 10-Q.
Final two: B beats A because Section 403 requires change reports by the end of the second business day, not on a monthly cycle.
Exam cue: an insider's change in holdings is due within two business days; the initial statement is due within 10 days.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. As-of date
questions.question: Management of a calendar-year company prepares its report on internal control over financial reporting. Under Section 404(a), as of which date must it assess effectiveness?

options.A: December 31, the end of the most recent fiscal year
options.B: Any date within 90 days before the annual report is filed
options.C: Across the whole fiscal year, from January through December
options.D: The date the audit firm signs its attestation report

questions.key_concept: Management assesses internal control over financial reporting as of the end of the most recent fiscal year.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether the assessment is a point-in-time conclusion or a period conclusion, and which point the statute names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(a) and Item 308(a) require management to assess the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting as of the end of the most recent fiscal year. For a calendar-year company that is December 31. The 90-day window appears in Section 302's text; SEC rules now set the officers' evaluation of disclosure controls at each quarter-end (Rule 13a-15(b)).

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 302's text speaks of an evaluation within 90 days. SEC rules now set disclosure controls evaluations at quarter-end, and 404(a) fixes the assessment at year-end.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing happens during the year. But the conclusion is stated as of a point in time, the fiscal year-end, not across the period.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the attestation follows the assessment. But the audit firm's signing date does not set management's as-of date; the fiscal year-end does.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The assessment is a point-in-time conclusion, and the audit firm's signing date does not set management's as-of date.
Final two: A beats B because Section 404(a) fixes the as-of date at fiscal year-end; the 90-day window is Section 302's original text, now replaced by quarter-end evaluations.
Exam cue: management's 404(a) assessment is as of fiscal year-end, even when testing runs throughout the year.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. The auditor's part
questions.question: Tamsin Freight is an accelerated filer, not an emerging growth company. Under Section 404(b), the registered public accounting firm that issues its audit report must:

options.A: Replace management's assessment with its own audit of controls
options.B: Sign a Section 302 certification, as the CEO and CFO do
options.C: Attest to management's assessment through a separate engagement
options.D: Attest to management's assessment within its audit engagement

questions.key_concept: Under Section 404(b), the firm that issues the audit report attests to management's internal control assessment, and the attestation may not be a separate engagement.
questions.pre_read: Think about who performs the assessment, who attests to it, and how the attestation relates to the audit.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 404(b) requires the registered public accounting firm that prepares or issues the issuer's audit report to attest to, and report on, management's internal control assessment under the PCAOB's attestation standards, and says the attestation shall not be the subject of a separate engagement. Tamsin is an accelerated filer and not an emerging growth company, so the attestation applies. Option C names the right duty in the wrong form: the attestation sits inside the audit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the auditor tests controls too. But Section 404(a) gives the assessment to management; the firm attests to that assessment and never replaces it.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because both are SOX duties tied to the annual report. But the CEO and CFO sign the Section 302 certifications; the auditor signs no certification.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the firm does attest to management's assessment, but Section 404(b) says the attestation shall not be the subject of a separate engagement.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the auditor attests to management's assessment rather than replacing it, and B, because only the CEO and CFO sign Section 302 certifications.
Final two: D beats C because Section 404(b) bars a separate engagement; the attestation is part of the audit by the firm that issues the audit report.
Exam cue: on 404(b) items check three things: an accelerated or large accelerated filer, not an emerging growth company, and the firm that issues the audit report, inside that audit.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Weakness fixed in the year
questions.question: In September, an accelerated filer finds a material weakness in revenue cutoff; replacement controls test effective at its December 31 year-end, and no other weakness is open. What may management MOST accurately conclude?

options.A: Controls were not effective, because a weakness existed before year-end
options.B: Controls were effective except for the revenue cutoff weakness
options.C: Controls were effective, as the weakness was remediated by year-end
options.D: No conclusion is possible until the auditor retests the new controls

questions.key_concept: A material weakness remediated and tested before fiscal year-end does not prevent an effective conclusion as of year-end.
questions.pre_read: Focus on the date the assessment speaks to, and on what the testing showed at that date.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 308(a) asks for management's assessment as of fiscal year-end, and management may not conclude controls are effective if a material weakness exists then. Release No. 33-8810 (Section II.A, footnote 20) says that if all material weaknesses found are remediated by fiscal year-end, management may conclude ICFR is effective as of year-end, but should consider whether disclosing the remediated weakness is appropriate or required under Item 307 or 308.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a material weakness did exist in September. But the assessment is as of year-end, and this one was remediated and tested by then.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems candid. But SEC guidance says management should not qualify its conclusion with exceptions; it states effective or not effective.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because auditors test controls too. But management makes its own year-end conclusion; the auditor's work does not delay or replace it.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. SEC guidance bars except-for conclusions, and management concludes on its own evidence without waiting for the auditor.
Final two: C beats A because the 404(a) assessment is as of year-end, and a weakness remediated and tested by then does not block an effective conclusion.
Exam cue: judge material weaknesses at the as-of date. Open at year-end means not effective; fixed and tested before it allows effective, though disclosing the fixed weakness should be considered.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Rating a failed review
questions.question: Management finds the review of large manual journal entries did not operate all year, yet no misstatement resulted, and the CFO says this cannot be a material weakness. Which response is MOST accurate?

options.A: Severity turns on the material misstatements actually found
options.B: Severity turns on the risk that a material misstatement is missed
options.C: Severity is set by the independent auditor, not by management
options.D: Severity turns on how many separate controls failed this year

questions.key_concept: Deficiency severity depends on the reasonable possibility of a material misstatement going unprevented or undetected, not on actual errors.
questions.pre_read: Recall what the material weakness definition measures: what happened, or what could happen.
questions.correct_explanation: A material weakness exists when there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis (Rule 12b-2). Release No. 33-8810 states that severity does not depend on whether a misstatement actually occurred. A key review that failed all year over large manual entries can be a material weakness even though no error was found.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: actual errors are strong evidence of a deficiency. But severity rests on what could be missed, so finding no misstatement does not settle it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because auditors assess deficiencies too. But management evaluates severity for its own 404(a) report under SEC rules and guidance.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because several failures can combine. But one failed control can be a material weakness; severity rests on likelihood and size, not a count.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Management rates severity for its own report, and severity depends on likelihood and magnitude rather than on counting failed controls.
Final two: B beats A because the definition asks whether a material misstatement could go unprevented or undetected, not whether one occurred.
Exam cue: when a stem says no error was found, ask what could have been missed; severity follows the potential, not the actual.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Committee without an expert
questions.question: A listed company's board determines that no audit committee member meets the SEC's definition of an audit committee financial expert. What does Section 407 require?

options.A: Disclose that the committee has none and explain why not
options.B: Disclose that the committee has none, giving no reasons
options.C: Appoint a qualified expert to the committee before filing
options.D: Name the committee's most experienced member as its expert

questions.key_concept: Section 407 is disclose-or-explain: name the financial expert, or state there is none and explain why.
questions.pre_read: Decide whether Section 407 requires the company to have an expert or to disclose something, and what that disclosure must include.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 407 and Item 407(d)(5) are disclose-or-explain rules. The company discloses whether the board has determined that at least one audit committee financial expert serves on the committee; if none does, it must say so and explain why. The Act does not require the company to have an expert, so the explanation, not an appointment, is what the rule demands.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the company must disclose that it has no expert. But Item 407(d)(5) also requires it to explain why it has none.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because an expert strengthens the committee. But Section 407 requires disclosure, not appointment; a company may lack an expert if it explains why.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because someone must fill the role. But the expert must have every attribute the SEC lists; naming an unqualified member would misstate the disclosure.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 407 requires disclosure rather than appointment, and a member without the SEC's attributes cannot be named as the expert.
Final two: A beats B because the rule requires an explanation of why the committee has no financial expert.
Exam cue: Sections 406 and 407 are disclose-or-explain: say whether you have it, and if not, say why.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Waiver for an officer
questions.question: A domestic issuer's board grants its CFO a waiver from the conflict-of-interest provision of its code of ethics for senior financial officers. What does Section 406 require?

options.A: Seek SEC approval of the waiver before it applies
options.B: Report the waiver in the next annual report on Form 10-K
options.C: Disclose the waiver immediately, on Form 8-K or online
options.D: Keep the waiver internal, since adopting a code is optional

questions.key_concept: Any change in or waiver of the code of ethics for senior financial officers must be disclosed immediately.
questions.pre_read: Separate the rule about having a code from the rule about changing or waiving one, and recall its timing.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 406(b) requires immediate disclosure of any change in or waiver of the code of ethics for senior financial officers. Under Form 8-K Item 5.05, a domestic issuer files within four business days, or posts the waiver on its website within four business days if its last annual report announced that method. Waiting for the next Form 10-K misses the deadline.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the SEC oversees disclosure. But Section 406 requires disclosure of the waiver, not SEC approval before it applies.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the annual report does cover the code. But waivers must be disclosed within four business days on Form 8-K or the website, not held for the 10-K.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because Section 406 is disclose-or-explain for adopting a code. But once a code exists, any waiver for senior financial officers must be disclosed.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Section 406 requires disclosure rather than SEC approval, and the disclose-or-explain choice on adopting a code does not cover waivers.
Final two: C beats B because Section 406(b) requires immediate disclosure of waivers, not disclosure in the next annual report.
Exam cue: a change in or waiver of the senior financial officers' code means immediate disclosure on Form 8-K or online.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Ethics code, financial expert, SEC review and real-time disclosure. Review cycle
questions.question: The CFO of a listed company that has filed Section 13(a) reports for years asks how often the SEC must review them. Under Section 408, what is the GREATEST interval allowed between reviews?

options.A: At least once every year
options.B: At least once every five years
options.C: Whenever a material restatement is issued
options.D: At least once every three years

questions.key_concept: The SEC must review each reporting issuer's disclosures at least once every three years.
questions.pre_read: Recall the statutory floor for SEC review and the role of the scheduling factors Section 408 lists.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 408 requires the SEC to review the disclosures of issuers reporting under Section 13(a), including their financial statements, on a regular and systematic basis. Section 408(c) sets the floor: no issuer may be reviewed less often than once every three years. Restatements, volatility and size are scheduling factors that can bring a review sooner, not the sole trigger.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many issuers are reviewed more often than the minimum. But Section 408 sets the floor at once every three years, not every year.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because five years appears elsewhere in SOX, in audit partner rotation. But Section 408 sets the review floor at three years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because restatements are a review factor. But Section 408(b) lists them as scheduling factors; the three-year floor applies to every reporting issuer.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Five years is not the review floor, and restatements only affect scheduling within the three-year cycle.
Final two: D beats A because Section 408(c) requires review at least once every three years; yearly review is not the statutory minimum.
Exam cue: SEC review of each reporting issuer's filings happens at least once every three years under Section 408.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 408 (Enhanced review of periodic disclosures by issuers)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Audit committees. Committee's own counsel
questions.question: Under Rule 10A-3, when a listed issuer's audit committee decides to hire its own independent counsel for an accounting inquiry, the issuer must:

options.A: pay the counsel from a budget the CFO sets for the committee
options.B: pay the counsel once shareholders ratify the engagement
options.C: pay the counsel at the funding level the committee determines
options.D: pay the counsel if the independent auditor agrees it is needed

questions.key_concept: The audit committee may engage independent advisers, and the listed issuer must fund them at the level the committee determines.
questions.pre_read: Ask who sets the money for the committee's own advisers, and whether anyone outside the committee must approve the hire.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10A-3(b)(4) gives the audit committee authority to engage independent counsel and other advisers it judges necessary, and Rule 10A-3(b)(5) requires the listed issuer to provide appropriate funding, as the committee determines, to pay them. Option A fails because a CFO-set budget would hand control of the committee's inquiry back to the management it may be examining.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the CFO usually manages budgets. But Rule 10A-3(b)(5) makes the committee decide the funding, so management cannot cap the committee's own advisers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because shareholders vote on some auditor matters. But Rule 10A-3 needs no shareholder vote on the committee's advisers; the committee decides and the issuer pays.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor reports to the committee. But the auditor has no say over the committee's advisers; the hiring authority and the funding decision are the committee's.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Rule 10A-3 asks for no shareholder vote on the committee's advisers, and the independent auditor has no say in whom the committee hires.
Final two: C beats A because Rule 10A-3(b)(5) lets the committee, not management, determine the funding for its advisers.
Exam cue: on audit committee resources, the committee decides and the issuer pays: for the auditor, for the committee's own advisers and for its running costs.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Officer leaves before filing
questions.question: Halden Corp's CFO resigns two days before its Form 10-Q is filed, and the controller takes over the CFO's duties in the interim. Under Rule 13a-14, who signs the Section 302 certification as financial officer?

options.A: The former CFO, who led finance throughout the quarter
options.B: The controller, who performs the CFO's functions at filing
options.C: The former CFO, through a power of attorney to the controller
options.D: The CEO, signing a second certification in place of the CFO

questions.key_concept: Section 302 certifications are signed by whoever holds, or performs the functions of, the principal executive and financial officer roles when the report is filed.
questions.pre_read: Note when the report is filed and who holds each officer role at that moment, not who held it during the quarter.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-14(a) requires each principal executive and principal financial officer, or person performing similar functions, at the time of filing to sign a certification. The controller, performing the principal financial officer's functions when the 10-Q is filed, signs. Option A fails because the former CFO no longer holds the role at filing, however long they led finance during the quarter.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the former CFO knows the quarter best. But Rule 13a-14(a) looks to the officers serving when the report is filed, and the CFO has left.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting as a way to keep the CFO's name on the report. But Rule 13a-14(c) forbids signing a certification on someone's behalf under a power of attorney.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the CEO already certifies. But Section 302 needs both the executive and the financial officer roles covered; the acting officer fills the financial role.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Rule 13a-14(c) bars signing through a power of attorney, and the CEO's certification cannot stand in for the financial officer's.
Final two: B beats A because Rule 13a-14(a) asks who performs the principal financial officer role at the time of filing.
Exam cue: for who signs a Section 302 certification, Rule 13a-14(a) looks to the officers in place, or acting, when the report is filed; no power of attorney.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. What the 906 statement says
questions.question: A CFO is drafting the Section 906 statement that will accompany a Form 10-Q containing financial statements. Which statement belongs in it?

options.A: The officers have evaluated disclosure controls and reported any fraud to auditors
options.B: Management assessed internal control as effective at year-end
options.C: The independent auditor has attested to management's internal control assessment
options.D: It fully complies with 13(a) or 15(d) and fairly presents operating results

questions.key_concept: The Section 906 statement certifies only that the periodic report fully complies with Section 13(a) or 15(d) and fairly presents condition and results.
questions.pre_read: List what each certification or report says, then match the two-part content of the criminal certification.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 18 U.S.C. 1350(b), added by Section 906, the statement certifies that the periodic report fully complies with Section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Exchange Act and fairly presents, in all material respects, the financial condition and results of operations. Option A describes the Section 302 certification's control and disclosure statements, which are not part of the 906 statement.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the CFO does certify this each quarter. But it belongs to the Section 302 certification; the 906 statement covers only compliance and fair presentation.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because officers stand behind controls. But management's effectiveness assessment is the annual Section 404(a) report, not part of any quarterly 906 statement.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because attestation adds assurance. But the attestation is a Section 404(b) report by the audit firm, not a statement the CFO signs.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. Management's control assessment is the annual Section 404(a) report, and the auditor's attestation is a Section 404(b) report, not an officer's statement.
Final two: D beats A because 18 U.S.C. 1350(b) limits the 906 statement to full compliance and fair presentation; control evaluations and fraud disclosures belong to Section 302.
Exam cue: two short promises, compliance and fair presentation, backed by criminal penalties point to 906; the long list about controls and disclosures points to 302.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Disclosure controls evaluation date
questions.question: Under Rule 13a-15(b), management of a domestic issuer, with its CEO and CFO, must evaluate the effectiveness of its disclosure controls and procedures:

options.A: as of the end of each of its fiscal quarters
options.B: as of each fiscal year-end, like its ICFR
options.C: as of a date within 90 days before each report
options.D: continuously, with a monthly report to the SEC

questions.key_concept: A domestic issuer evaluates disclosure controls as of each fiscal quarter-end; ICFR is assessed as of fiscal year-end.
questions.pre_read: Separate disclosure controls from ICFR, and domestic issuers from foreign private issuers, before choosing the evaluation date.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 13a-15(b) requires management, with the principal executive and financial officers, to evaluate disclosure controls and procedures as of the end of each fiscal quarter, and Item 307 reports the officers' conclusions. Option C repeats the Act's original wording in Section 302(a)(4)(C); the current rule keeps a 90-day window only for registered investment companies.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Section 302(a)(4)(C) of the Act does say within 90 days. But Rule 13a-15(b) now fixes quarter-end for issuers; the 90-day window remains only for registered funds.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because ICFR is assessed yearly and foreign private issuers evaluate disclosure controls yearly. A domestic issuer evaluates them every quarter.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because disclosure controls run all the time. But the rule sets a point-in-time evaluation each quarter, and there is no monthly report to the SEC.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. Year-end evaluation is the rule for ICFR and for foreign private issuers, and no monthly report to the SEC exists.
Final two: A beats C because Rule 13a-15(b) sets each fiscal quarter-end for a domestic issuer; the 90-day wording survives only for registered funds.
Exam cue: disclosure controls, each quarter-end; ICFR, fiscal year-end; foreign private issuers evaluate disclosure controls yearly.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Officer certifications: Sections 302 and 906. Disclosure committee
questions.question: A newly listed company's general counsel says the SEC requires a disclosure committee to support the officers' Section 302 certifications. What did the SEC say on this when adopting its certification rules?

options.A: It required one, chaired by the principal financial officer
options.B: It required the audit committee to serve as the disclosure committee
options.C: It recommended one but required no particular review procedures
options.D: It discouraged one, since the signing officers alone evaluate controls

questions.key_concept: The SEC recommended, but did not require, a disclosure committee to help the certifying officers judge materiality and meet disclosure deadlines.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the certification rules require of the signing officers from what the SEC only suggested companies consider.
questions.correct_explanation: In Release No. 33-8124 (August 2002), the SEC said it was not requiring any particular procedures for the officers' review and evaluation, but recommended that issuers create a committee to consider the materiality of information and decide disclosure obligations on time, reporting to senior management. Option A turns that suggestion into a mandate with a set chair, which the release never did.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many companies form one, often led from finance. But Release No. 33-8124 only recommended a committee and set no required chair or membership.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the audit committee oversees reporting. But the SEC pictured a management committee reporting to the senior officers, not a board committee.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the officers certify personally. But the SEC encouraged a committee to help them; the officers keep responsibility for the evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: B and D. The SEC pictured a management committee that reports to the signing officers, and it encouraged rather than discouraged one.
Final two: C beats A because Release No. 33-8124 recommended a disclosure committee without making it, or any chair, a requirement.
Exam cue: when an option turns an SEC suggestion into a rule, check the source's verb: recommends is not requires.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Who enforces audit-influence rules
questions.question: A shareholder plans a civil suit against a former CFO who misled the company's auditor in breach of Section 303. Under that section, who may enforce it in a civil proceeding?

options.A: Any harmed shareholder, through a private civil lawsuit
options.B: The PCAOB, which oversees the audit firm that was misled
options.C: The audit committee, through a lawsuit on the company's behalf
options.D: The SEC, which holds exclusive authority in civil cases

questions.key_concept: In civil proceedings, only the SEC may enforce Section 303 and its rules against improperly influencing the auditor.
questions.pre_read: Look for who the statute names as enforcer, and whether it shares that role in civil cases.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 303(b) gives the SEC exclusive authority to enforce Section 303 and its rules in any civil proceeding, so no private party can bring a civil claim under it. Option A fails for that reason; a harmed shareholder must rely on other laws, which Section 303(c) expressly leaves in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: shareholders can sue under other securities laws. But Section 303(b) reserves civil enforcement of Section 303 to the SEC alone.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the auditor was the target. But the PCAOB oversees audit firms, not issuer officers; Section 303 is the SEC's to enforce.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the committee oversees the auditor. But a board committee cannot enforce a federal statute; Section 303(b) names the SEC.

tips: Eliminate: B and C. The PCAOB oversees audit firms rather than issuer officers, and an audit committee cannot enforce a federal statute.
Final two: D beats A because Section 303(b) makes the SEC's civil enforcement authority exclusive, leaving no private claim under that section.
Exam cue: Section 303 protects the auditor from officers and directors, and its only civil enforcer is the SEC.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Standard for an officer bar
questions.question: Under the standard set by Section 305, a federal court may bar a person who violated the antifraud rules from serving as a public company officer or director if their conduct shows:

options.A: substantial unfitness to serve as an officer or director
options.B: unfitness to serve as an officer or director of any issuer
options.C: intent to defraud, proven beyond a reasonable doubt at trial
options.D: fraud serious enough to have led to a criminal conviction

questions.key_concept: Section 305 lowered the standard for a court-ordered officer and director bar from substantial unfitness to unfitness.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Section 305 changed in the bar standard and what kind of case the bar comes from.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 305(a) struck substantial unfitness from Exchange Act Section 21(d)(2) and Securities Act Section 20(e) and inserted unfitness, so a court may bar a violator whose conduct demonstrates unfitness to serve as an officer or director of an issuer. Option A states the higher standard that applied before 2002.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this was the test before the Act. Section 305 removed the word substantial, making bars easier for the SEC to obtain.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a bar feels like punishment. But it comes from a civil action; the court looks for unfitness, not criminal proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because convictions often lead to bars. But the civil bar needs no prior conviction, only conduct showing unfitness.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. These bars come from civil actions, so neither criminal proof beyond a reasonable doubt nor a prior conviction is needed.
Final two: B beats A because Section 305 replaced substantial unfitness with unfitness in both the Exchange Act and the Securities Act.
Exam cue: Section 305 lowered the bar for a bar: unfitness, no longer substantial unfitness.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 305(a) (Unfitness standard); 15 U.S.C. 78u(d)(2) (Authority of court to prohibit persons from serving as officers and directors)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Audit influence, forfeiture, bars and blackout periods. Telling insiders about a plan freeze
questions.question: Riverside Mills gets the ERISA notice of a 10-business-day freeze on all participants' company-stock trades in its 401(k), its only individual account plan. Under Regulation BTR, when must it notify its directors and executive officers?

options.A: At least 30 days before the freeze, as participants are told
options.B: Within two business days after the freeze begins
options.C: At least 15 calendar days before the freeze begins
options.D: Within five business days after receiving the notice

questions.key_concept: An issuer that receives the plan administrator's blackout notice must notify its directors and executive officers within five business days.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the issuer received the plan administrator's notice; the deadline for telling insiders depends on that fact.
questions.correct_explanation: 17 CFR 245.104(b)(2) treats notice to directors and executive officers as timely if given no later than five business days after the issuer receives the plan administrator's ERISA notice. Option C is the fallback used only when no such notice reaches the issuer: at least 15 calendar days before the blackout begins.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Regulation BTR does use 15 calendar days. But only when the issuer receives no plan notice; here the notice arrived, so five business days applies.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because ERISA gives participants 30 days' advance notice. That is the plan administrator's duty to participants, not the issuer's deadline for insiders.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because insiders report trades within two business days. That is the Section 16 deadline, and notice after the freeze starts would come too late.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. Thirty days is ERISA's notice to participants, and two business days is the Section 16 trade-report deadline.
Final two: D beats C because 17 CFR 245.104 uses the 15-day fallback only when the issuer never receives the plan administrator's notice.
Exam cue: a Section 306 blackout carries two notices: the plan tells participants under ERISA, and the issuer tells its directors, executive officers and the SEC.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Attorneys and fair funds. Reporting to a compliance committee
questions.question: An in-house lawyer reports evidence of a material violation to the company's qualified legal compliance committee. Under Section 307 and the SEC's rules, what remains of the lawyer's reporting duty?

options.A: It has been met, and the lawyer need not assess the response
options.B: It continues until the response is judged appropriate
options.C: It continues until the lawyer also reports the evidence to the SEC
options.D: It has been met, unless the chief legal officer rejects the report

questions.key_concept: A lawyer who reports evidence of a material violation to a qualified legal compliance committee has met the duty and need not judge the response.
questions.pre_read: Compare the standard up-the-ladder route with the alternative route a qualified legal compliance committee offers.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 17 CFR 205.3(c)(1), adopted under Section 307, a lawyer may report evidence of a material violation to a previously formed qualified legal compliance committee instead of following the standard ladder. Doing so satisfies the reporting obligation, and the lawyer need not assess the issuer's response. Option B describes the standard route, where the lawyer must judge whether the response was appropriate.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: on the standard ladder the lawyer must weigh the response. But reporting to a qualified legal compliance committee ends that duty under 205.3(c)(1).
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the SEC enforces the rule. But Section 307 sets an internal reporting ladder, and nothing in it makes the lawyer report to the SEC.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the chief legal officer leads the standard route. But a report to the committee bypasses that officer and itself satisfies the duty.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 307's duty runs inside the company, not to the SEC, and the chief legal officer cannot reopen a duty already met.
Final two: A beats B because 205.3(c)(1) frees a lawyer who reports to a qualified legal compliance committee from assessing the response.
Exam cue: when the stem names a qualified legal compliance committee, the lawyer's reporting job ends once the report reaches it.
questions.framework_ref: 17 CFR 205.3(c) (Reporting to a qualified legal compliance committee); Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 Section 307 (Rules of professional responsibility for attorneys)

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Auditor-identified corrections
questions.question: Under Exchange Act Section 13(i), added by Section 401(a), an issuer's financial report containing financial statements filed with the SEC must reflect:

options.A: every correcting adjustment the auditor proposes, material or not
options.B: all material correcting adjustments the independent auditor has identified
options.C: the adjustments the audit committee approves before the filing date
options.D: management's adjustments, with the auditor's disputed ones in the notes

questions.key_concept: Financial statements filed with the SEC must reflect every material correcting adjustment the registered public accounting firm identifies.
questions.pre_read: Notice who identifies the adjustments and whether the duty reaches immaterial ones.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 401(a) added Exchange Act Section 13(i): each financial report with GAAP financial statements filed with the SEC must reflect all material correcting adjustments identified by a registered public accounting firm under GAAP and SEC rules. Option A drops the materiality limit; the statute reaches material corrections, not every entry the auditor proposes.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it names the right source of the adjustments. But Section 13(i) covers material correcting adjustments, not every entry the auditor proposes.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the committee oversees reporting. But the statute ties the duty to corrections the audit firm identifies, not to committee approval.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because disagreements are sometimes disclosed. But Section 13(i) requires the statements themselves to reflect material corrections, not a note listing them.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The duty follows the audit firm's identified corrections, not committee approval, and a note cannot replace booking a material correction.
Final two: B beats A because Section 13(i) is limited to material correcting adjustments the registered firm identifies.
Exam cue: in Section 401, watch for the word material: material corrections, material off-balance-sheet arrangements, no misleading pro forma figures.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Guarantee of an unconsolidated venture
questions.question: Coral Bay Energy guarantees an unconsolidated joint venture's bank debt, which could materially affect its liquidity. Under Exchange Act Section 13(j), added by Section 401(a), how must its CFO treat it in Coral Bay's reports?

options.A: Disclose it in each annual and each quarterly report filed
options.B: Disclose it in the annual report but not in quarterly reports
options.C: Disclose it once it is called and a loss is booked
options.D: Leave it out while the joint venture stays unconsolidated

questions.key_concept: Material off-balance-sheet arrangements, including contingent obligations such as guarantees, must be disclosed in each annual and quarterly report.
questions.pre_read: Ask which reports carry off-balance-sheet disclosure and whether an obligation must first turn into a loss.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 401(a) added Exchange Act Section 13(j), directing SEC rules so that each annual and quarterly financial report discloses all material off-balance-sheet transactions, arrangements and obligations, including contingent obligations, with unconsolidated entities that may have a material current or future effect. Option B wrongly limits the duty to the annual report.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the annual report does carry it. But Section 13(j) reaches each annual and quarterly report, so the 10-Qs must disclose it too.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a contingent loss may not be booked yet. But Section 13(j) covers contingent obligations that may have a material future effect.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the venture sits off the balance sheet. That is exactly the kind of arrangement Section 13(j) brings into the reports.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. Section 13(j) reaches contingent obligations before any loss, and unconsolidated status is the reason to disclose, not an exemption.
Final two: A beats B because Section 13(j) applies to each annual and each quarterly report.
Exam cue: off-balance-sheet disclosure under Section 401 follows both the 10-K and the 10-Q, and includes guarantees not yet called.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Periodic report disclosures and insider dealings. Adjusted figure in an earnings release
questions.question: Fernhill Retail, a U.S. domestic listed company, issues an earnings press release that leads with adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure. Under Rule 100(a) of Regulation G, what must the release also present?

options.A: A statement that the adjusted figure is unaudited and not GAAP
options.B: The independent auditor's review report on the adjusted figure
options.C: The most comparable GAAP measure, with a quantitative reconciliation
options.D: No reconciliation until the figure appears in an SEC filing

questions.key_concept: A public non-GAAP measure must come with the most directly comparable GAAP measure and a reconciliation, wherever it is released.
questions.pre_read: Notice the channel, a press release rather than a filing, and recall what must sit beside a non-GAAP figure.
questions.correct_explanation: Regulation G, adopted under Section 401, requires a registrant that publicly discloses material information including a non-GAAP measure to present the most directly comparable GAAP measure and a quantitative reconciliation of the differences (17 CFR 244.100(a)). Option D fails because the rule reaches any public disclosure, including press releases, not only SEC filings.

wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: many assume only SEC filings are covered. But Regulation G applies to any public disclosure, so the press release itself needs the reconciliation.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because adjusted figures are often unaudited. But a label does not replace the comparable GAAP measure and reconciliation the rule requires.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because auditors review quarterly results. But Regulation G asks the company for a GAAP comparison and reconciliation, not an auditor's report on the measure.

tips: Eliminate: A and B. A label cannot replace the GAAP comparison, and Regulation G puts the duty on the company, not on an auditor's report.
Final two: C beats D because Regulation G covers every public disclosure of a non-GAAP measure, press releases included.
Exam cue: a non-GAAP figure made public anywhere needs its closest GAAP measure and a reconciliation beside it.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Where the evaluation starts
questions.question: Planning its first Section 404(a) evaluation, a manufacturer's SOX team proposes to start by listing every control in every process. Under SEC Release 33-8810, where should management's evaluation begin?

options.A: With the controls the independent auditor tested in its audit
options.B: With a full inventory of controls across every business process
options.C: With the risks that could cause a material misstatement
options.D: With IT general controls over each application in use

questions.key_concept: Management's ICFR evaluation is top-down: identify risks of material misstatement first, then the controls that adequately address them.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the SEC's guidance puts first: risks to the financial statements or an inventory of controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Release No. 33-8810 Section II.A.1 says the evaluation begins with identifying and assessing financial reporting risks, those that could result in a material misstatement, then asks whether controls adequately address them, considering entity-level controls. Option B is the bottom-up inventory the guidance does not require; management need not identify every control in a process.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a full list feels thorough. But Release No. 33-8810 says management need not identify every control; it starts from risks and focuses on the controls that address them.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the auditor's work is available. But management makes its own evaluation, starting from its financial reporting risks, not from the auditor's test plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because systems feed reporting. But IT general controls come in only where key controls depend on them, after the risks are identified.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Management's evaluation is its own, not the auditor's test plan, and IT general controls matter only where key controls rely on them.
Final two: C beats B because the 2007 guidance starts from financial reporting risks and does not require identifying every control.
Exam cue: top-down, risk-based means the statements and their risks first, then the controls that address them; never a bottom-up control census.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Support for the assessment
questions.question: Management of a large accelerated filer concludes ICFR is effective based on process owners' verbal confirmations, keeping no records of its testing. What does Item 308 require of management?

options.A: Evidential matter, including documentation, that supports its assessment
options.B: Written documentation of every control in each process that affects reporting
options.C: Nothing further, as the independent auditor documents the testing
options.D: Filing its testing workpapers as an exhibit to the Form 10-K

questions.key_concept: Management must keep evidential matter, including documentation, that reasonably supports its ICFR assessment, focused on the controls that address financial reporting risks.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what management must keep for its own conclusion against what the auditor keeps and what is filed with the SEC.
questions.correct_explanation: Instruction 2 to Item 308 requires management to maintain evidential matter, including documentation, that provides reasonable support for its ICFR assessment, and Release No. 33-8810 adds that its form and extent vary with the company's size, nature and complexity. Option B overshoots: the guidance says documentation need not cover every control in a process, only those that address financial reporting risks.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: documentation is required. But Release No. 33-8810 says it need not include every control, only those management relies on to address financial reporting risks.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the auditor keeps workpapers. But the auditor's files support its own opinion; management must keep support for its own assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because evidence feels like something to file. But Item 308 requires management to maintain the support, not to file it with the 10-K.

tips: Eliminate: C and D. The auditor's workpapers support the auditor's opinion, not management's assessment, and Item 308 asks management to keep its support, not file it.
Final two: A beats B because the 2007 guidance focuses documentation on the controls that address financial reporting risks, not on every control.
Exam cue: management's assessment needs its own reasonable support: evidence and documentation kept by management and focused on the controls that matter.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Management's assessment of internal control. Mid-year system change
questions.question: In its third fiscal quarter, an issuer's finance team moves billing to a new system, materially changing its revenue controls. Under Item 308(c), what must its third-quarter Form 10-Q disclose about the change?

options.A: Management's assessment of ICFR effectiveness as of the quarter-end
options.B: The change in internal control that materially affected its ICFR
options.C: Nothing about the change until the annual ICFR assessment
options.D: The independent auditor's attestation on the new system's controls

questions.key_concept: Each quarterly and annual report discloses any change in ICFR during the last quarter that materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, ICFR.
questions.pre_read: Separate the annual effectiveness assessment from the quarterly duty to report material changes in internal control.
questions.correct_explanation: Item 308(c) requires each quarterly and annual report to disclose any change in ICFR during the last fiscal quarter that materially affected, or is reasonably likely to materially affect, ICFR, found in the quarterly evaluation under Rule 13a-15(d). Option C treats ICFR as a purely annual matter, but material changes are reported quarter by quarter.

wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the effectiveness assessment is annual. But Item 308(c) still requires each 10-Q to disclose material changes in internal control during the quarter.
wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the change is significant. But management's effectiveness assessment under Section 404(a) is made as of fiscal year-end, in the annual report.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the auditor will test the new system. But any 404(b) attestation appears in the annual report, never in a 10-Q.

tips: Eliminate: A and D. Effectiveness assessments and auditor attestations come once a year in the annual report, not in a quarterly report.
Final two: B beats C because Item 308(c) makes every 10-Q disclose material changes in internal control during that quarter.
Exam cue: quarterly reports tell what changed in ICFR; the annual report says whether ICFR works.
